Incredible Addition to HL2**

There is no way to undercut this DLC. It is absolutely phenomal and even a casual visitor (such as this reviewer) will likely relish every moment spent playing it, quirks and all. Any return to the Half Life universe is most welcome. This installment begins with the player loading in at precisely the moment HL2 ended. As you can imagine, this only helps deepen the immersion of the journey.

The story of Episode One is the driving force, and well it should be: storytelling seems to take on a new prominence, even for Valve. HL2 was one of the first games in recent memory that made so complete and compelling use of NPCs to really advance the story. The writing, direction and pacing of the story not only continues to be first rate: it actually gets better. That didn't seem possible given how utterly fantastic HL2 is, but Valve found a way to do it. Facial animations are unreal (remember, this DLC originally came out in 2005-6) and the voice acting is incredible. AND THIS IS A FREAKING SHOOTER. If this genre is supposed to inspire the feelz, shouldn't it be limited to excitement and anticipation? Not an emotional rollercoaster of tension, fear, relief, wonder and suspense?

Speaking of being a shooter, the level of difficulty is increased accordingly. While not insurmountable, those players who had been looking for more of a challegne should be pleased: Episode One returns players to a time when combat decisions matter. More use of the functions of the HEV suit (flashlight, oxygen, etc) and some good puzzles/lateral thinking help here, as well. Also, there is noticeably less ammunition. It's no longer possible to blast your way through EVERY problem encountered. A bit of finesse (or fleet-footedness) will be required.

**But for all these changes, there were some struggles. At times, it feels as though Episode One shines a spotlight on some of the things HL2 struggled with. It was very cool to learn more about Alyx and watch her character develop. It was far less cool to watch her do virtually everything of consequence in the game. As a player, it's frustrating to have nearly every action (for story or game play progression) require NPC input. At this point, we've watched Gordon Freeman (the only 'theoretical physicist' who can single-handledly take out entire teams of Recon Marines, Delta Force-level goons, previously unknown armored alien vehicles like Striders and more) solve every problem thrown at him. To 'need' someone else to open every door for him, or tell him where to go seems a bit... contrived. Forced. Less fun. Advancing the goals of humanity was, until this point, a task left almost entirely in the hands of one person. But suddenly, someone else is required to help. It also seems a disservice to Alyx, as she is strong and capable. Does she really need Gordon to do these things? No, and that makes the relationship seem insincere at times. In those moments, it's not about seeing Gordon and Alyx struggle and grow together; it's about having a semi-emotional vehicle that attempts to justify itself as a means to shoe-horn the story forward. 

Regardless of the criticism offered in this review, it must be remembered that this content is still well worth the investment (in finances and time). That statement is true of any addition to the HL franchise, be it episodic, stand-alone or even only tangentially related (Portal, et al). Similarly, even with these few subjectively negative oberservations, Episode One is a part of one of the best, most powerful and enduring franchises in video game history. Not only that, but it is part of an amazing progression in storytelling, as well. Conceptually, the HL universe is compelling and completely engrossing. This DLC continues in that tradition beautifully... even if that beauty is marred by a miniscule, nigh-on microscopic blemish.

8/10. Incredible. Episode One is head and shoulders better than many of its peers in the FPS genre. Peers that are full-fledged, core/base games that take tens of hours to complete, not a DLC/add-on that takes a mere handful of hours to play through.

Looking at the overwhelmingly positive reviews, it's clear I'm in the minority here when I give it a thumbs down, but I really could not enjoy this game like I did Half Life 2.

We'll start with the negatives and work our way to the positives as I want to end this on a optimistic note. The game starts off okay, nothing crazy good but to rag on the details would be nitpicking. Where it starts to fall off is the 3rd level "Lowlife". To describe, it's essentially a dark and destroyed (parking lot I believe?) and you have to use your flashlight along the way to illuminate your obstacles. This on paper sounds fine, but you have to remember your flashlight has charge. This means that one minute, your cruising along with Alyx blasting away zombies, the next your sitting the dark looking at your pistol LEDs wondering if the battery always took this long to charge. It just makes the pacing feel awkward.

Soon in to the level a new enemy is introduced, called the "Zombine" by Alyx. The only good thing I can say about them is that the name made me chuckle. It's unfortunate because I really like the idea of them, but it just wasn't introduced right. See, one way of attacking is using a grenade to suicide bomb you. This is fine, but not dark corridors where explosive barrels surround you. I mean hey, one wrong misfire at a barrel and you won't have to worry about the place being dark anymore, right? Both the map design here and the Zombine resulted in me getting blown up, and half the time I wouldn't know where or when and sometimes how.

Proceeding deeper into the level we'll encounter the antlions again, only this time they're not our friends anymore. The problem I have was in Half Life 2 they'd only be triggered if you stepped in the sand, which made you think outside of the box and be creative with movement. In this, they keep constantly spawning, in order to stop this you plug them up with usually a car or truck. Again, like the Zombine I like this idea but they end up becoming a chore to do, meanwhile you constantly get hit by antlions while doing it.

Once we get to "Urban Flight" the game gets better, but not by much. The design for this level felt awkward to me, there was one part where the Combine were guarding a gate, and as far as I know, the only way to get in was to charge in guns blazing when the door was occasionally open. For Half Life, this part felt so unnatural, I never think of Half Life as a "run and gun" FPS like Doom, it's more "take your time to think outside the box" type of FPS. Maybe you'll see this as a nitpick, I'll leave it up to you to determine that. 

The rest of the game proceeds fine, but by then were almost at the end. Which is where my final big complaint comes in, for how short this game is, as well as its age, the price doesn't feel worth it. I got this from a Half Life bundle where I got everything Half Life for about 5 or 10 bucks, but 8 bucks for this? You're better spending your money elsewhere, or wait for a sale.

Now for the positives! For a short game, a lot of story happens and I'm really happy about that. It was enough to keep me engaged and motivated when the gameplay let me down at times. And the ending makes me eager in playing Episode Two. To help progress the story, Alyx accompanies you throughout the game and she is a great companion! My favorite thing about her is that she can hack Rollermines to attack the enemy instead which is a cool gameplay idea! (It's just unfortunate it doesn't happen more, maybe in the next episode we get more)

...And that's all the positives I got. It's unfortunate because I really wanted to like this game, especially after a masterpiece like Half Life 2. But I look forward into the next episode with optimism.

I enjoyed the episode immensely. I played the game a few hours a sitting over the course of three nights. Getting all achievements was really fun. Happy I came back to it in 2021 after playing on the release, great memories. If you are a fan of Half Life universe this is a "must have". It may also even surprise new players if you a enjoy a good game despite its age.

[h1]I give Half-Life 2: Episode One a 9.5/10[/h1]

Half-Life 2: Episode One takes place in the aftermath of Half-Life 2, you play as Gordon Freeman, an MIT graduate with a background involving the black mesa incident and a member of the human resistance. After the citadel's teleporter was destroyed, it started a chain reaction of chaos, and destruction to the once named, City 17. Now you and your partner, Alyx Vance must escape the ruins of city 17 before the citadel self-destructs, but that's easier said than done.
[list]
[*]The levels show the ruins of City 17 in a fun, and creative way
[*]New Enemy thats proves a great challenge
[*]More puzzles involving with the laws of physics and combat strategy
[*]New "boss battle" scenarios with other creatures and/or vehicles
[*]First game to heavy work with HDR (High Dynamic Range) lighting which proves to improve the Half-Life experience
[*]Improved AI compared to Half-Life 2
[*]Great soundtrack
[/list]

Episode 1 continues where Half Life 2 ended.

It's the shortest one of them all and adds a few new things which I really like for instance Alyx can only see in the dark if you turn on the flashlight and point it in some direction.

A must have for a Half-Life fan of course.

The release of this Episode signified a hope of something bigger coming in the near future. We got that with The Orange Box and Episode Two wouldn't have been possible without the evolution the Half-Life architecture went through in Episode One.

It's evident that this installment is mainly about Alyx, her emotions, reactions and her relationship with Gordon. In the beginning, she is delighted to find you amidst the rubble. She is given a lot of space to express her anxiety about going back inside the Citadel to delay the reactor's core's meltdown and whispers your name at the very end of the Episode.

She is your companion and will stand by your side through most of the game. Her AI and reactivity were improved a ton as she is very helpful, moves away when she gets in your way, and you can count on her during the more precarious situations. In the chapter Lowlife when you are left wandering through pitch black underground garages, you will have to cooperate with Alyx by using light sources like your flashlight to illuminate zombies so that she can shoot them.

There are no new weapons, just the good old Valve creativity. They added flares that can light zombies on fire. Antlions now spawn from burrows that can be sealed with car wrecks using the Gravity Gun and a new combination of an armored Combine soldier and a zombie dubbed Zombine is present. Graphically the game's lighting was drastically improved with the addition of HDR.

The overall mood of the game is again top-notch. The landmark of Citadel is now a looming threat of catastrophic proportions. City 17 is more ruined than ever. I spent a long time just brooding over the destroyed cityscape and listening to Dr. Kleiner's emergency broadcast turned motivational speech.

"For what the Combine fear the most is not any tangible human weapon, but our will, our intellect, our ability to respond selectively and rationally to every terror they turn against us. We place our firmest hope in the human spirit, even knowing how easily it may be shattered."

9/10

+ Alyx's emotional maturity and improved AI set a new milestone for video game companions, the true Half-Life atmosphere enhanced by apocalyptic imminence, Zombines and their distorted voices, excellent soundtrack, prepares the ground for the next Half-Life adventure
- extremely short (can be beaten in under 3 hrs)

Half-Life 2: Episode One picks up directly from its predecessor, delivering a seamless and gripping extension of Gordon Freeman's journey through the dystopian world of City 17. Episode One continues with effortlessly blending immersive storytelling, captivating gameplay mechanics, and stunning visuals into an exhilarating gaming experience.

The beauty of Episode One is its ability to maintain the momentum and intensity established in [i]Half-Life 2[/i]. Valve masterfully captures the sense of urgency and desperation as Gordon and Alyx navigate through the city's crumbling infrastructure, constantly on the run from the relentless Combine forces.

The relationship between Gordon Freeman and Alyx Vance takes centre stage. Alyx's unwavering loyalty and resourcefulness make her an indispensable ally, and the chemistry between her and Gordon is palpable. The dynamic between the two protagonists adds layers of depth to their partnership and enhances the overall narrative experience.

In addition to its compelling storytelling, Episode One introduces several new gameplay mechanics that keep the action fresh and exciting. The introduction of [i]Stalkers[/i] and the [i]Zombines[/i] add a new level of challenge, requiring players to adapt their strategies and utilize the environment to outsmart their adversaries. The inclusion of [i]Dark Energy[/i] mechanics further enhances the gameplay experience, allowing players to manipulate objects and solve puzzles in creative ways.

The attention to detail is evident throughout the episode, from the crumbling architecture of City 17 to the eerie atmosphere of the underground tunnels. The Source engine shines with its ability to deliver realistic lighting effects and immersive environments, further absorbing players in the world of [i]Half-Life[/i].
Episode One plays alongside a wonderfully crafted, haunting soundtrack that complements the game's atmosphere well. The sound effects are, as expected, top notch. From the ominous hum of Combine machinery to the intense gunfire of enemy soldiers, every segment of audio feels accurately crafted to enhance the overall experience. 

Overall, [i]Half-Life 2: Episode One[/i] continues the triumphant series in remarkable fashion. It’s quite possibly the [i]ninth[/i] or [i]tenth[/i] time I’ve finished this, and it still blows my mind how ahead of its time these games were. Valve cements their mastery of the FPS genre, delivering an experience that is both exhilarating and emotionally resonant.

Half-Life 2: Episode One is kind of the black sheep of the Half-Life 2 games. It is a good game in it’s own right but it lacks the innovation of Half-Life 2 and it lacks the story of Episode 2 which is by far the best story arc of the whole series in my eyes. So we are left with a good game that is sadly forgotten in the mix by many because it is the middle child. All of the same great game play is back in Episode One. The story in itself is good and enjoyable. City 17 is now a war zone and the game revolves around trying to escape it. The graphics are just as good as Half-Life 2, no better but no worse. The game doesn’t have any of the driving sections of the original. There is however a great level taking place in a hospital which was almost as creepy as Ravenholm.

	I played Episode One on Linux. It never crashed on me. There are once again some AI issues. This time what happened to me was on a mission where I have to lead civilians to a departing train some of them got stuck in a wall corner and wouldn’t proceed making me have to reload a previous save. Outside of the AI issue I noticed no other bugs.  There were 4 AA settings; 6 AF settings; a V-Sync toggle; 9 other graphics options and an FOV slider that went from 75-90. You could change the difficulty level at any time as well as manually save at any time. Performance was fantastic which wasn’t surprising given the game’s age.

	Overall I can’t say too many negative things about Episode One. It does it’s job well which is to further the Half-Life story. It doesn’t innovate but it also doesn’t make anything worse. I finished the game on the hardest difficulty in 3 hours and 48 minutes.

Ok, let's start with an excellent base of half-life 2.

Now let's add escorting that lasts basically the entire game.

Then add levels where your flashlight - which is attached to a battery system that your sprint is also attached to - is required. This lasts for several chapters.

Then give the return of antlions, but rather than keeping the prior canon of them knowing where you are via vibrations in HL2, here that doesn't apply, and the way you counter them is putting a car on their spawn points so it doesn't become a shitty L4D2.

The parts where your alone in the Citadel and the part where you're alone after escort final boss are easily the best parts. But those are right at the start of the game and very near the end of the game.

It's Half Life 2, but with shitter level design. What I've played of HL2 Ep2 is easily better than Ep 1 so far.

However, this review was also touched by me playing the game with the "One True Bullet" achievement in mind, which would have made certain sections, like the aformentioned areas of darkness, much easier and more fun for me than "shine area with light, let Alyx shoot enemies there" that I did.

This is a terrible game because it is the worst thing a game can be: simply not fun. A game should, by definition, be something that you enjoy, and this feels like a chore. A shooter game in which half the time you have nothing to shoot enemies with, either because you have no guns or you have no ammunition? Wow, what a great idea!

And the repetitiveness is just terrible. Just how many cars do I have to push into holes to stop an endless stream of antlions? That thing got old the moment it appeared, but no, they make you do it again and again.

So you say you don’t like doing the same stuff over and over again? Great, because we have an electronic door for which you have to find the switch somewhere in the pitch dark. And when you do it, there is another. And another. And another. Yeah, we are really lazy when building levels so guess what? There is a group of people you have to escort from A to B. And when you do it, go back to A, because there is another group to escort to B. Then you will have to do it again. And after that, guess what you have to do? That’s right, the same thing again. And then again, just for good measure.

Plus, present (or rather, absent) are the same things that plague the whole series: no map, no coherent storyline (lack of coherent story is spun to mean “ambiguous” and “ambiguous” is spun to somehow mean great), and often no clear objectives, so you will easily find yourself not quite knowing where you should go, while not quite knowing what to do and definitely not knowing why. Granted, the situation is better here than in the first Half-Life game, but worse than in Half-Life 2.

And during the whole time, the game offers you a giant middle finger from developers in the form of “witty” remarks from Alyx, in which she (or rather they) mock you for doing all the stupid repetitive things the game makes you do, while not having any of the things I mentioned in the above paragraph (Alyx, by the way, got extremely annoying extremely fast). “Too bad we don’t have a map”, Alyx says at one point; “Wow, this again”, at another; “Good thing you know what to do, Gordon” in a situation when you don’t know what to do, except that you should somehow stop the core from exploding. On the surface, I guess this is supposed to be tongue in cheek, but in reality it is a giant FU to the player. “See, we make you do stupid things in a lousy game; we make fun of you for doing it; and you are gonna love us and convince yourself that this is a great game.” And sadly, many people do.

Play this only if you got it for free and you hate yourself.

Don't get me wrong, Half-Life 2: Episode One is still a *good* game, but it isn't great. Certainly not nearly as great as it was made out to be back when it was first released. It progresses the story of Half-Life 2 at the cost of interesting or fresh gameplay. While that might seem obvious, when actually experiencing it - the game just doesn't *do* much that doesn't feel quite repetitive. It's 2023, so the style of HL2 and the gunplay it provides are now rather old and very much overplayed in terms of the heaps of other FPS games with action that could easily be pointed to as a derivative of what Valve's Source engine was providing at the time of ~2006. The way Valve tells a story through the Half-Life franchise has long been widely considered as a crown-jewel of story-driven FPSs. So, it's no surprise that upon replay it doesn't shine as brightly as it did in the 2006-07 era. But even given those dampened expectations, the experience the game provides was still disappointing upon replay 15+ years later. 

I'm not even sure the additional story is worth the 3 hours I spent if more than 1/3 of it I found pretty uninteresting. That said, given the popularity around Episode Two, 3 hours is not much to ask. Play through it over a holiday break when you've got a sleepy day or few to yourself with more hours than you know what to do with. Otherwise, I'd probably pass on it. 

I recommend it to Half-Life fans or those who really insist playing through Episode 2. Plus, I am a huge Half-Life fan after-all...

On the otherhand, if you do not fall into the above mentioned groups - then just pass on it. It really isn't that ground breaking of a sequel, nor does it provide a lot of content to enjoy. 3 hours for $7.99 (at the time of writing this) isn't that great of a deal. Ultimately, I will give it a thumbs down because the cons just stack too high.

Episode 1 is the odd middle child of the Half Life 2 family. While not as flushed out as Episode 2, it is still an enjoyable and integral piece of the Half Life 2 puzzle. It is a more puzzle oriented game in the beginning, with you having to do a lot of dodging and ducking eventually opening up into something more relatable to what you experienced in Half Life 2. 

Episode 1 almost plays like an extended Ravenholm as the Grav Gun is the central focus of gameplay from the beginning of the game, and arguably throughout the remainder. That is not to say there isn’t room for some good gunplay, but it is to say that I beat the entire game firing only a single bullet and using the Grav Gun for the remainder.

The crumbling ruins of City 17 are an awesome site to behold. Dr. Kleiner's voice resonates messages of hope as well as warning throughout the city while rebels attempt to flee and the Combine infrastructure collapses. The ending arrives rather abruptly, and turns into a rather tedious and short escort mission. It is at this point where the game starts to feel a bit rushed to the conclusion. In the end Episode 1 is more reminiscent of an expansion pack than a stand alone game.

A must have for completionists, and to appreciate the wonderful story of Half Life 2, even if you only play through it once.

This is clearly not a flaw, but it does feel as if they had initially planned more content and then scrapped a bit of that and made transitions between different "biomes" a lot shorter than would feel natural. Half Life 2 Episode 1 is honestly a relic of it's time.

Nowadays this game is just bundled into HL2 so if you want to play this. That's the best way.
